propositions.text: Applicant seeks to overturn two negative PRRA decisions finding no risk if returned to Honduras
propositions.quote: The Applicant, Ricardo Antonio Lopez Alvarez, seeks to overturn two negative Pre-Removal Risk Assessment (PRRA) decisions that found him not to be at risk if he returned to Honduras.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant seeks to overturn two negative PRRA decisions finding no risk if returned to Honduras, says the court.

propositions.text: First negative PRRA decision made before officer reviewed documents provided by Applicant
propositions.quote: The first negative PRRA decision was made before the officer had an opportunity to review documents provided by the Applicant.

propositions.text: Decision reviewed again after new documentation; addendum issued finding no risk of persecution or mistreatment
propositions.quote: Following that review, a PRRA Decision – ADDENDUM was issued, which found that the Applicant had not established that he faced a risk of persecution or mistreatment if he returned to Honduras.

paragraphs.summary: The first PRRA decision was made before reviewing documents; after review, an addendum found no risk, says the court.

propositions.text: Applicant challenges both decisions; second decision is an addendum incorporating first decision's reasons
propositions.quote: The Applicant challenges both decisions and, by agreement of the parties, the matters were heard together. In reality, the second PRRA decision is simply an addendum to the first, and so the “reasons” for the second decision incorporate those provided for the first.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant challenges both decisions; second is an addendum incorporating first decision's reasons, says the court.

propositions.text: Applications for judicial review are dismissed
propositions.quote: For the reasons set out below, the applications for judicial review are dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the applications for judicial review.

propositions.text: Applicant is Honduran citizen who came to Canada in 2011 under temporary foreign workers program
propositions.quote: The Applicant is a citizen of Honduras. He came to Canada in August 2011 under the temporary foreign workers program.

propositions.text: Applicant returned to Canada in 2012 but lost job in 2013 due to medical condition
propositions.quote: He returned to Canada in August 2012, but by June 2013 he had lost his job because he was unable to work due to a medical condition.

propositions.text: Applicant married Canadian citizen in June 2013
propositions.quote: He married a Canadian citizen in June 2013.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant is Honduran citizen who came to Canada in 2011, lost job in 2013 due to medical condition, and married a Canadian citizen, says the court.

propositions.text: Applicant's work permit expired July 2013; exclusion order issued August 2013
propositions.quote: The Applicant’s work permit expired in July 2013, and an exclusion order was issued against him in August 2013.

propositions.text: Applicant applied for permanent residence in January 2014 under spouse class; processing suspended due to 2017 convictions
propositions.quote: In January 2014, he submitted an application for permanent residence under the spouse or common-law partner in Canada class. The processing of that application was suspended, however, because in June 2017 the Applicant was convicted of driving while impaired and for failure to comply with an undertaking.

propositions.text: Deportation order issued August 2017
propositions.quote: A deportation order was issued against the Applicant in August 2017.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant's work permit expired in 2013; exclusion order issued; permanent residence application suspended after 2017 convictions; deportation order issued, says the court.

propositions.text: Applicant submitted PRRA application December 2017 alleging risk due to imputed political opinion and association with National Party
propositions.quote: The Applicant submitted a PRRA application on December 12, 2017, alleging risk in Honduras on the basis of his imputed political opinion as a municipal employee of the city of San Lorenzo and his association with the National Party.

propositions.text: Applicant claimed harassment and threats from opposition alleging municipal corruption involvement
propositions.quote: He claimed that he had faced harassment and threats from members of the opposition who alleged that he was involved in municipal corruption.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant submitted PRRA alleging risk from imputed political opinion and opposition threats, says the court.

propositions.text: Applicant obtained supporting documents in Spanish, arranged translation, provided to Respondent March 22, 2018
propositions.quote: The Applicant obtained supporting documentation from his family in Honduras, but it was all in Spanish. He arranged for translation of these documents, and his counsel provided them to the Respondent on March 22, 2018.

propositions.text: Applicant received call-in notice March 9, 2018 for April 3 meeting to receive PRRA decision
propositions.quote: On March 9, 2018, he had received a “call-in” notice from the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) for a meeting on April 3, 2018, in order to receive the decision on his PRRA.

propositions.text: Applicant's counsel contacted CBSA officer to explain further documents submitted; April 3 meeting cancelled
propositions.quote: The Applicant’s counsel contacted the CBSA officer to explain that he had provided further documentation, and the officer cancelled April 3, 2018 meeting.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant provided translated documents March 22, 2018; April 3 meeting cancelled after counsel's explanation, says the court.

propositions.text: Applicant received new call-in notice for April 25, 2018 meeting; received first negative PRRA decision dated March 2, 2018
propositions.quote: The Applicant then received another call-in notice for a meeting on April 25, 2018. At that time, he received the first negative PRRA decision, dated March 2, 2018, which did not take into account the further material his counsel had submitted.

propositions.text: Applicant advised removal scheduled for July 3, 2018; removal later cancelled
propositions.quote: The Applicant was advised that his removal from Canada had been scheduled for July 3, 2018. The removal was later cancelled,

propositions.text: Parties agreed PRRA officer would reconsider decision per Chudal case, considering March 2018 documents
propositions.quote: the parties agreed that based on the decision in Chudal v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2005 FC 1073, the PRRA officer would reconsider the decision and take into account the documents the Applicant had submitted in March 2018.

propositions.text: Application for leave and judicial review of first PRRA decision held in abeyance by agreement
propositions.quote: The parties also agreed that the application for leave and judicial review of the first PRRA decision (IMM-2128-18) would be held in abeyance.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant received first negative PRRA decision ignoring new documents; removal scheduled then cancelled; parties agreed to reconsider decision and hold review in abeyance, says the court.

propositions.text: Applicant received second negative PRRA decision August 7, 2018; removal scheduled August 20, 2018
propositions.quote: The Applicant received the second negative PRRA decision on August 7, 2018, and his removal was scheduled for August 20, 2018.

propositions.text: Removal stayed by order of this Court
propositions.quote: The removal was stayed by Order of this Court.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant received second negative PRRA decision August 7, 2018; removal scheduled then stayed by court order, says the court.

propositions.text: Second PRRA decision styled as addendum focusing on new evidence; must be read with first decision
propositions.quote: The second PRRA decision is styled as an “addendum” to the first. It does not repeat all of the analysis set out in the first decision, but rather focuses on the new evidence. The two decisions must be read together.

paragraphs.summary: Second PRRA decision is an addendum focusing on new evidence and must be read with the first, says the court.

propositions.text: First PRRA decision recounts Applicant's immigration history and basis of PRRA claim
propositions.quote: The first PRRA decision begins by recounting the Applicant’s immigration history and notes that he based his PRRA application on his fears of returning to Honduras because of his imputed political opinion and his association with the National Party and the municipal government of San Lorenzo.

propositions.text: Applicant provided evidence of robbery and message warning him not to stay in Honduras
propositions.quote: He had provided evidence that his mother’s home had been robbed and that a message had been left for the Applicant stating that he “should not even think about staying in Honduras.”

propositions.text: Applicant was attacked and hospitalized for six days; officer accepts this evidence
propositions.quote: The Applicant states that he was attacked a short time later, during which he was threatened and ended up in hospital for six days. The officer accepts this evidence.

propositions.text: Assailants unknown to Applicant or police; no allegations about suspects
propositions.quote: However, the officer notes that the assailants were unknown to the Applicant or the police and he had not made any allegations about who he suspected they were.

paragraphs.summary: First PRRA decision recounts Applicant's history, evidence of robbery, attack, and notes assailants unknown, says earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: Applicant did not provide evidence of National Party membership, municipal employment, or family political profile
propositions.quote: The officer states that the Applicant had not provided any evidence to establish that he was a member of the National Party or had been employed by the municipal government or that his mother or family have any political profile in Honduras.

propositions.text: Robbery and attack not evidence of prospective risk due to imputed political opinion or employment
propositions.quote: Therefore, the robbery and attack were not evidence that he faced a prospective risk of harm because of his imputed political opinion or his employment.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence shows attacks against political candidates, leaders, activists and families
propositions.quote: The documentary evidence indicated that armed attacks and homicides had occurred against political candidates, leaders of parties, and activists and their families.

propositions.text: Applicant did not demonstrate he fit political profile of person at risk in Honduras
propositions.quote: The officer found the Applicant had not demonstrated that he fit the political profile of a person at risk of being targeted in Honduras.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found no evidence Applicant was National Party member or at political risk, despite attacks on political figures, says earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: National Party won last election and government took office despite disputes
propositions.quote: The officer notes that the National Party had won the last national election and, although many citizens disputed the results, the government had nevertheless taken office.

propositions.text: Objective evidence did not support Applicant's claim of personalized risk
propositions.quote: The objective evidence did not support the Applicant’s claim that he faced a personalized risk.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found National Party in power and no objective evidence supporting Applicant's personalized risk claim, says earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: Applicant did not provide evidence of opposing gangs or facing particularized risk
propositions.quote: the officer concludes that the Applicant had not provided evidence to support that he had opposed gangs, or otherwise faced such risks.

propositions.text: Evidence showed Applicant faced generalized risk of violence like others in Honduras
propositions.quote: Rather, the evidence showed that the Applicant faced the same generalized risk of violence as others in Honduras.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found no evidence Applicant opposed gangs; risk was generalized violence like others, says earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: Applicant's desire to remain in Canada due to family not relevant to PRRA assessment
propositions.quote: the officer notes the Applicant’s desire to remain in Canada because his wife and children live here, but found that this was not a consideration for a PRRA assessment;

propositions.text: Family considerations could form basis for separate humanitarian and compassionate application
propositions.quote: rather, this could form the basis for a separate humanitarian and compassionate application.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found Applicant's family ties irrelevant to PRRA but relevant to separate humanitarian application, says earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: Officer rejected PRRA application
propositions.quote: For these reasons, the officer rejected the PRRA application.

paragraphs.summary: Officer rejected the PRRA application, says earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: Same PRRA officer reconsidered application after additional evidence; second decision styled as addendum
propositions.quote: Following the receipt of the additional evidence the Applicant submitted, the same PRRA officer reconsidered the application. The resulting decision is styled “PRRA Decision – ADDENDUM.”

propositions.text: Second decision focuses on new evidence and incorporates first decision
propositions.quote: It focuses on the new evidence that the Applicant provided in late March 2018, and does not repeat all of the earlier decision. As noted above, the second decision effectively incorporates the first and builds upon it, and so the decisions will be treated together.

paragraphs.summary: Same officer reconsidered application with new evidence; second decision styled as addendum incorporating first, says the court.

propositions.text: Documents confirmed Applicant's political activity, National Party affiliation, and municipal employment
propositions.quote: The officer notes that several documents had been provided, which confirmed the Applicant’s political activity and affiliation with the National Party, and that he had been a municipal employee of San Lorenzo.

propositions.text: National Party currently in power in Honduras after winning national election
propositions.quote: The officer also notes, however, that the National Party was currently in power in Honduras, having won a four-year term in a national election.

propositions.text: Officer accepts Applicant was National Party member and former municipal worker, and victim of opposition persecution in 2011
propositions.quote: I accept that the applicant was a member of the National Party and that he was a former government worker for the municipality of San Lorenzo. I also accept that he was a victim of persecution, harassment, threats and intimidation by the opposition party in 2011;

propositions.text: Applicant has not lived in Honduras for over six years; insufficient evidence opposition would harm him now
propositions.quote: I also note that the applicant has not lived in Honduras for more than six years. I have been provided with insufficient evidence that the opposition party or anyone would be interested in harming him six years following his departure from Honduras.

propositions.text: Applicant provided insufficient evidence; no more than mere possibility of persecution or risk of torture or cruel treatment
propositions.quote: Therefore, without sufficient supporting evidence for this application I am left to conclude that on a forward looking basis, the applicant would not face more than a mere possibility of persecution in Honduras nor is he more likely than not to face a danger or (sic) torture, or a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

propositions.text: Application failed to meet requirements of sections 96 and 97 of IRPA; application rejected
propositions.quote: The application has failed to meet the requirements of Section 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. The application is rejected.

paragraphs.summary: Officer accepts Applicant's past political activity but finds insufficient evidence of current risk; application rejected under IRPA sections 96 and 97, says earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: Issue is whether second PRRA decision is reasonable; challenge to first decision subsumed
propositions.quote: The only issue in this case is whether the second PRRA decision is reasonable. The challenge to the first PRRA decision (IMM-2128-18) is subsumed in this, because the second decision incorporates and expands upon the first.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the issue is whether the second PRRA decision is reasonable; challenge to first decision is subsumed.

propositions.text: At the time of argument, Dunsmuir v New Brunswick was the leading authority on reasonableness review.
propositions.quote: When this case was argued, the leading authority on reasonableness review was Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9, and its progeny.

propositions.text: Since then, the Supreme Court updated the judicial review framework in Vavilov and related cases.
propositions.quote: Since then the Supreme Court of Canada has updated and clarified the framework for judicial review in Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 [Vavilov] as applied in Bell Canada v Canada (Attorney General), 2019 SCC 66, and Canada Post Corp v Canadian Union of Postal Workers, 2019 SCC 67 [Canada Post].

paragraphs.summary: The court states that Dunsmuir was the leading authority on reasonableness review when argued, but the Supreme Court updated the framework in Vavilov and related cases.

propositions.text: No need for additional submissions on standard of review; Vavilov framework applies and yields same result as Dunsmuir here.
propositions.quote: In view of paragraph 144 of Vavilov, I see no reason on the facts of this case to request additional submissions from the parties on either the appropriate standard or the application of that standard.

propositions.text: Canada Post held it was not unfair to apply Vavilov framework when argued under Dunsmuir if result is the same.
propositions.quote: This case is similar to the situation in Canada Post, where the Supreme Court stated at paragraph 24 that it was not unfair to decide a case applying the Vavilov framework when it had been argued under the Dunsmuir approach, because under both frameworks the result would be the same.

paragraphs.summary: The court decides no further submissions are needed; applying Vavilov is fair and yields the same result as Dunsmuir, per Canada Post.

propositions.text: The standard of review for PRRA decisions is reasonableness, unchanged by Vavilov.
propositions.quote: The standard of review that applies to the merits of the PRRA decisions is reasonableness. This standard has been applied in previous decisions (Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at para 43 [Khosa]; Rahman v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 941 at para 17). This has not changed under Vavilov.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the reasonableness standard applies to PRRA decisions and remains unchanged by Vavilov.

propositions.text: Reasonableness review asks if decision shows justification, transparency, intelligibility, and rational analysis.
propositions.quote: When reviewing for reasonableness, the Court asks “whether the decision bears the hallmarks of reasonableness – justification, transparency and intelligibility – and whether it is justified in relation to the relevant factual and legal constraints that bear on the decision” (Vavilov at para 99). It must be internally coherent, and display a rational chain of analysis (Vavilov at para 85).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains reasonableness review requires justification, transparency, intelligibility, and rational analysis per Vavilov.

propositions.text: A decision is unreasonable if reasons and record do not show reasoning on a critical point.
propositions.quote: As such, a decision will be unreasonable if the reasons read in conjunction with the record do not enable the Court to understand the decision maker’s reasoning on a critical point (Vavilov at para 103).

propositions.text: Vavilov affirms the need for a culture of justification in administrative decision-making.
propositions.quote: The framework set by this decision “affirm[s] the need to develop and strengthen a culture of justification in administrative decision-making” by endorsing an approach to judicial review that is both respectful and robust (Vavilov at paras 2, 12-13).

paragraphs.summary: The court states a decision is unreasonable if reasons lack clarity on critical points and Vavilov promotes justification culture.

propositions.text: The PRRA officer misapprehended the nature of the risk alleged and did not consider evidence reasonably.
propositions.quote: The core of the Applicant’s argument is that the PRRA officer misapprehended the nature of the risk he alleged, and therefore did not consider the evidence in a reasonable manner.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the PRRA officer misunderstood the risk and failed to reasonably consider the evidence.

propositions.text: Applicant faced threats and accusations linked to corruption, fled Honduras in 2011, was attacked in 2012.
propositions.quote: The Applicant alleged that he faced a risk of persecution as a member of the National Party and a municipal employee. The evidence showed that he had faced threats and accusations from opposition members who linked him to the corrupt practices of the former mayor, and accused him of stealing money from the poor. This led him to flee Honduras and to come to Canada as a temporary foreign worker in 2011. When he returned to Honduras in 2012, his mother’s house was robbed, and he was physically attacked and ended up in hospital.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges he faced threats as a National Party member and municipal employee, fled Honduras, and was attacked on return.

propositions.text: Officer failed to consider objective country condition evidence showing rampant gang violence and targeting of municipal officials.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the officer failed to consider the objective documentary evidence that shows that gang violence and extortion is rampant in Honduras, and that municipal officials have been targeted because of this.

propositions.text: Reports at decision time showed evolving migration patterns and gang violence in Honduras.
propositions.quote: At the time the PRRA officer made his decision, there were several reports that demonstrated the way in which migration patterns in the region had evolved, including the Amnesty International report Home Sweet Home: Honduras, Guatemala and El Salvador’s Role in a Deepening Refugee Crisis (2016), as well as the report of the Research Directorate of the Immigration and Refugee Board, Honduras: Information Gathering Mission Report (2018).

propositions.text: Officer’s failure to consider risk in light of country evidence makes decision unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The Applicant’s position is that the officer’s failure to consider his alleged risk in light of the specific country condition evidence makes the decision unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the officer ignored country evidence of gang violence and municipal targeting, making the decision unreasonable.

propositions.text: Officer failed to consider wider risk from gang violence demographic profile and lack of state protection.
propositions.quote: In addition, the Applicant argues that the officer failed to consider the wider risk of harm he faced because he fit into the demographic profile of the people being targeted by gang violence.

propositions.text: Country evidence shows state protection unavailable and risks to returnees and municipal workers from gangs.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the country condition evidence shows that state protection is not available in Honduras, and that gang violence and threats are rampant in the country. The evidence shows risks to people returning to Honduras from abroad, as well as risks to persons who work in activities susceptible to extortion, including municipal workers and those who do not comply with a gang’s authority.

propositions.text: Officer’s failure to analyze this evidence makes decision unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The officer’s failure to engage in any meaningful analysis of this evidence makes the decision unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the officer ignored risks from gang violence demographics and lack of state protection, making the decision unreasonable.

propositions.text: PRRA officer considered evidence and affidavit in light of applicant’s claims; conclusions supported by evidence.
propositions.quote: The PRRA officer considered the evidence submitted in light of the claims advanced by the Applicant and the affidavit evidence he filed in support. The decision is based on an assessment of the sufficiency of the evidence in relation to these claims, and the officer’s conclusions are supported in the evidence.

propositions.text: Officer applied correct legal tests; decision and addendum show clear, coherent reasoning justifying conclusion.
propositions.quote: The officer applied the appropriate legal tests to the assessment of the evidence, and the decision – meaning the original decision plus the addendum – displays clear and coherent reasoning that justifies the conclusion reached.

propositions.text: This meets the Vavilov framework requirements for reasonableness review.
propositions.quote: This is what is required by the Vavilov framework for reasonableness review.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer considered evidence properly, applied correct legal tests, and gave clear reasoning meeting Vavilov standards.

propositions.text: Officer referred to applicant’s risk allegations and did not misapprehend their nature.
propositions.quote: The PRRA decision refers to the specific allegations of risks made by the Applicant and there is no basis to find that the officer misapprehended the nature of these claims.

propositions.text: PRRA analysis requires focus on forward-looking risk of harm (Kioko v Canada).
propositions.quote: The officer correctly focused on whether the evidence established a forward-looking risk of harm because that is what is required by a PRRA analysis (Kioko v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 717 at para 8).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer did not misunderstand the claims and properly focused on forward-looking risk as required by PRRA law.

propositions.text: Officer noted National Party was in power and opposition threats had ceased after applicant left Honduras.
propositions.quote: In relation to the claim that the Applicant faced risks as a person aligned with the National Party and from a family that had been politically active in Honduras, the officer rightly noted that the National Party had won power in contested elections and was continuing as the government at the time.

propositions.text: Evidence showed applicant was municipal employee and victim of opposition threats and harassment.
propositions.quote: Indeed, the further evidence he submitted included a number of statements by officials affirming that he had been an employee of the municipality of San Lorenzo, and that he was a victim of harassment, threats, and persecution by the opposition party.

propositions.text: No evidence threats continued after applicant left or that anyone searched for him due to municipal involvement.
propositions.quote: However, there was no evidence that these threats had continued after he left the country, or that anyone was continuing to search for him because of his prior involvement in municipal affairs.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer correctly noted the National Party's power, opposition threats ceased, and no ongoing threats to applicant.

propositions.text: Gang violence and extortion are significant problems; mayors face threats from gangs.
propositions.quote: The evidence shows that gang violence and extortion are significant problems in Honduras, and there is evidence that mayors face threats from gangs.

propositions.text: Officer concluded applicant did not show continued risk as former municipal employee; supported by evidence.
propositions.quote: The officer’s conclusion that the Applicant had not demonstrated that he faced a continued risk as a former municipal employee is supported in the evidence.

propositions.text: No evidence of continued threats against applicant; mother’s fears relevant but not decisive.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, there was no evidence of continued threats made specifically against the Applicant in the intervening period. The fact that his mother had expressed fears because of her involvement in municipal politics is a relevant but not decisive consideration.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds gang violence is serious but officer reasonably concluded applicant showed no continued personal risk.

propositions.text: Officer’s assessment of generalized violence risk in Honduras is well grounded in evidence.
propositions.quote: Finally, the officer’s assessment of the generalized risk of violence in Honduras is well grounded in the evidence.

propositions.text: Officer acknowledged serious crime and violence but found insufficient evidence of personal risk.
propositions.quote: In the decision, the officer states: “While acknowledging that crime and violence are serious concerns in Honduras, the applicant provided insufficient evidence of a personal risk.”

propositions.text: Conclusion based on evidence and generalized nature of applicant’s fears.
propositions.quote: This conclusion is also based on the evidence in the record and flows form the generalized nature of the fears expressed by the Applicant in his PRRA application.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer’s conclusion of insufficient personal risk despite serious crime is supported by evidence and applicant’s generalized fears.

propositions.text: PRRA officers must focus on actual risks alleged and link country evidence to personalized risks (Debnath v Canada).
propositions.quote: A PRRA officer is required to focus on the actual risks alleged by the individual, and these must be examined in the context of the evidence as a whole, including the specific evidence put forward by the claimant as well as the general country conditions documents. The approach is summarized by Justice Cecily Strickland in Debnath v Canada (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship), 2018 FC 332: [33] In this matter, the Officer addressed the letter of the Principal Applicant’s friend and then referred to their remaining submissions which included various news articles and country reports, noting that s 161(2) of the IRP Regulations required the Applicants to indicate how that evidence related to them. The Officer stated that the Applicants’ submissions described the general country conditions in Bangladesh but that they had not linked this evidence to their personalized, forward-looking risks. The Officer stated that it is well established that it is insufficient to simply refer to country conditions in general without linking them to the personalized situation of an applicant. Further, that the assessment of an applicant’s potential risk of being persecuted or harmed if sent back to his country, must be individualized. The fact that the documentary evidence shows that the human rights situation in a country is problematic does not necessarily mean that there is risk to a given individual. The Officer stated that the Applicants had not provided objective documentary evidence to support that their profile in Bangladesh is similar to those persons that currently face persecution, a danger of torture or a risk to life, or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in that country. The Officer concluded by stating that he or she found that the submissions related to conditions faced by the general population, or described specific events or conditions faced by persons not similarly situated to the Applicants.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Debnath: PRRA officers must link country evidence to personalized risks, not just general conditions.

propositions.text: Officer did not need to assess state protection because insufficient evidence of Convention-based risk.
propositions.quote: In the case at bar, the Applicant pointed to country condition evidence that shows that state protection is not available or effective in Honduras. However, I agree with the Respondent that the officer did not need to engage in a state protection analysis because there was insufficient evidence that the Applicant faced risks based on Convention grounds.

propositions.text: Officer acknowledged crime and violence concerns but state protection analysis was unnecessary.
propositions.quote: The officer acknowledged that crime and violence are serious concerns in Honduras, but it was not necessary for the officer to assess whether state protection was available and effective.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees the officer did not err by not assessing state protection due to insufficient Convention-based risk evidence.

propositions.text: Much evidence of risks to mayors, journalists, activists did not apply to applicant’s profile.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Respondent that much of the evidence of the situation in Honduras and the risks faced by particular groups simply did not apply to the Applicant; this includes risks faced by mayors, journalists, human rights defenders, and environmental activists.

propositions.text: Applicant’s profile does not fit these categories; generalized gang violence risks are not personal to him.
propositions.quote: The Applicant’s profile while he was in Honduras and since that time does not bring him within any of these categories, and the more generalized risks of gang violence are not personal to the Applicant.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the applicant’s profile does not match groups at risk; generalized gang violence is not personal risk.

propositions.text: Officer noted applicant’s family are Canadian citizens but impact of removal is separate and not determinative in PRRA.
propositions.quote: The officer notes that the Applicant’s wife and children are Canadian citizens, but that a consideration of their circumstances and the impact of possible removal of the Applicant must be done in the context of a separate process and is not determinative in relation to a PRRA assessment.

propositions.text: No error in officer’s conclusion on family circumstances and PRRA assessment.
propositions.quote: There is no error in this conclusion.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no error in the officer’s conclusion that family circumstances are not determinative in PRRA assessment.

propositions.text: Applications for judicial review IMM-2128-18 and IMM-4076-18 are dismissed.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, the applications for judicial review in IMM-2128-18 and IMM‑4076‑18 are dismissed.

propositions.text: No question of general importance for certification.
propositions.quote: There is no question of general importance for certification.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the judicial review applications and finds no question of general importance for certification.
